narrativeProgression.description: Bernard Jenkin argues that a parliamentary vote on Article 50 is not necessary, as treaties are made and unmade by prerogative power. He emphasizes that the Repeal Act will address citizens' rights and obligations. He views the UK's control over its finances, borders, laws, and parliamentary sovereignty as non-negotiable principles. He asserts that the government's agreements with the EU can be changed in the future, marking a significant shift from the UK's previous commitment to EU regulations.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: It could go one of two ways. We could have quite a close cooperation still maintain access
to the single market, a sort of Norway Switzerland type issue arrangement. But it could be that
Europe says, right, okay, we don't particularly want those deals and we do actually a WTO deal,
go back to those type of deals. I can't really tell you at this moment exactly what will happen.
I, though I was a remainder, I wouldn't go cap in hand. Europe is difficult. I think we should go our
own way. Germany wants to sell us cars. The French will sell us wine. The European Central and Eastern
Europeans will want to send their labour. So I think and we will need that labour. So there is a
deal to be done. I just hope that Europe can do one with us without feeling they've got to be so
careful that they don't get other people wanting to leave the European Union. If they give us
too good a deal, you see others will probably choose the same path. Some things are already very clear.
David Davis has made clear that we're going to take back control of our borders, our laws, and that
are money and Parliament's sovereignty is going to be put beyond doubt. And from that, actually a
number of things flow by implication. It means we're not going to be subject to the European Court
of Justice in any way. We're not going to be subject to European Union regulation. We're not
going to be in the EEA. We're not going to be in the Customs Union. We're not going to be in the
single market. These are logical outcomes from those premises.
I think that probably in the spring is about the right time to trigger article 50.
Parliamentary debate, I think we can have one, whether it should be binding or not is another
matter. I think we should debate it, but I think the referendum has been had, and so therefore people
have made that decision. And so therefore I feel the government and the country we are bound to
go the Brexit route. But I think the politicians of all sides would probably like to have their say,
but I think have their say, but not making a binding vote as to whether we went for article 50 or not.
I think we should debate the fact that we are invoking article 50, but not it's not a vote that
could be, not an article that could be stopped. Whether they're should or shouldn't is entirely a
political matter. It's not a legal question. Treaties are made and unmade by prerogative power.
The fact that this treaty may make or unmake private rights and private obligations on
citizens in this country is actually incidental. In any case, it's the repeal act that requires
the consent of Parliament. And it's the repeal act that will actually change the nature of
obligations in the future. And in case I hope the repeal act will also include a carry-over
provision, so we effectively nationalise the ACU commuter. So people will notice very little change
at the moment we leave the European Union.
Well, it is access to the market in a way either through a single market process or through a trade
arrangement, which is beneficial both to ourselves and to Europe. Also maintaining a controlled
control workforce coming in from Central and Eastern Europe because I in my own constituency
have quite a number of factories in particular and establishments which need central and Eastern
European labour. So there is a deal to be had. Let's hope that Europe will be sensible and we can
get that deal. Well, in that first category of principles set out by David Davis in his statement,
the day we got back. Money borders, laws and the sovereignty of Parliament. There's nothing to
negotiate. And we need to make a division in our minds. What is now constitutionally part of
the sovereign responsibility of the British Government and the British Parliament is a separate question
from what agreements might be made on a bilateral basis in the future. And I'm quite relaxed
about that because whatever is agreed by the government isn't binding for all time, it can be
changed in the future, which is the big change from leaving the European Union because when we
are in the European Union we'd agree something and it would be agreed for all time unless we left the
European Union.

youtube_description:
Senior Conservative MPs Neil Parish and Bernard Jenkin speak to DeHavilland about the UK’s decision to leave the EU and what happens next.

In this second video, both men set out what the UK Government must secure in the Article 50 negotiations with Brussels.

DeHavilland’s Brexit Intelligence packages can support your planning: https://www1.dehavilland.co.uk/brexit.
